correctness.rationale: For composite n the least prime p is at most √n, so small-divisor pairing gives τ≤2p+2 for nonsquares and τ≤2p+1 for squares exactly; in the latter case τ is odd. Prime n=p and all squares are negligible for fixed p. In the nonsquare factorization pᵉ∏qⱼ^{aⱼ}, the product (e+1)∏(aⱼ+1)≤2(p+1) bounds all exponents and gives at most uₚ=floor(log₂(p+1)) additional distinct primes. At maximal support with every aⱼ=1, the exact exponent bound is Eₚ=floor((p+1)/2^{uₚ−1})−1∈{1,2}. Allowed integers of this form are nonsquares and satisfy the exact criterion irrespective of the primes' sizes. Landau at X/pᵉ gives their common asymptotic scale and coefficient p^{−e}/(uₚ−1)!; restricting finitely many small primes does not affect it. For repeated exponents, split the product D of the at least square prime powers at √X. Below the split, sum 1/D against the fixed-r Landau bound, with r<uₚ first-power primes and log(X/(pᵉD)) of order log X. Above it, one qᵃ>X^{1/(2s)} with s repeated-prime factors; even counting all integer bases gives a union bound Oₚ(X^{1−1/(4s)}) by summing X/qᵃ. With r=0, the cofactor n/pᵉ is squarefull, and writing it as A²B³ with B squarefree gives O(√X) by summing B^{−3/2}. Terms with fewer simple primes also have lower order (including p-powers when uₚ=1). Thus only the stated simple-cofactor layers contribute, not necessarily all integers with maximal distinct support. An independent trial-division and direct-small-divisor calculation gave agreement for all 199,999 n from 2 through 200,000, including the square boundary at 16 and 729 and the nonsquare boundary at 12 and 135; it also confirmed the leading-layer inclusions checked for p=2,3,5,7.
residual_risks: The finite calculation verifies arithmetic predicates and examples, not a limit. The proof uses the classical Landau asymptotic and is not uniform as p grows.

evidence: The exact criterion immediately gives Eₚ for the maximal squarefree-cofactor patterns, but support alone does not rule out repeated primes among maximal-support integers. For example, p=5 allows both n=5²qr and n=5q²r for distinct primes above 5; the first contributes to the main term, the second has lower order. A sum over bounded higher-power patterns with an explicit tail, not simply dropping all non-squarefree cofactors, establishes that separation.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The method is elementary once the known inputs are assembled. The scientific increment is not a rediscovery of Landau's scale, but a uniform-in-form classification of the missing same-order layer and a correction of a quantitatively incorrect comparison, with the cofactor-pattern error now justified. It is not an already supplied special case of the inspected source statements.

originality.rationale: The divisor criterion, the support cutoff and the Landau scale are credited to prior work. The contribution is the corrected exact leading term: the motivating source's Corollary 1 proof uses an asymptotic comparison with only the p-times-squarefree-cofactor layer. As written this comparison misses another layer of the very same asymptotic order for many p, including 2. The result locates precisely the primes admitting this layer and bounds the repeated-cofactor-prime patterns away from the leading order. No inspected prior result already gives this corrected fixed-p coefficient.
residual_risks: No original Landau scan was inspected. The bounded search does not exclude an independent explicit correction elsewhere under another arithmetic counting formulation.

value.rationale: This is a natural sharpening of an existing count on exactly the fixed-prime strata already isolated in the motivating paper. The extra factor 1+1/p when the p² layer is allowed does not vanish as X grows for fixed p, and is 3/2 at p=2. Correcting that leading term and determining exactly which exponent layers may be ignored is substantive, even though the counting tool is classical. The iterated-log separation makes the strata quantitatively distinguishable; a density-zero statement alone does not.
residual_risks: This does not estimate the total Schreier count or provide a uniform approximation in the least prime. The significance is the corrected local asymptotic, not a new prime-distribution theorem.
